verses.text: It is indeed unnecessary for me to write to you concerning the service to the saints,
for I know your readiness, of which I boast on your behalf to them of Macedonia, that Achaia has been prepared for a year past. Your zeal has stirred up very many of them.
But I have sent the brothers that our boasting on your behalf may not be in vain in this respect, that, just as I said, you may be prepared,
so that I won’t by any means, if anyone from Macedonia comes there with me and finds you unprepared, we (to say nothing of you) should be disappointed in this confident boasting.

I thought it necessary therefore to entreat the brothers that they would go before to you, and arrange ahead of time the generous gift that you promised before, that the same might be ready as a matter of generosity, and not of greediness.
Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart; not grudgingly, or under compulsion; for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.
As it is written, “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.”
Now may he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, supply and multiply your seed for sowing, and increase the fruits of your righteousness;
you being enriched in everything to all liberality, which produces through us thanksgiving to God.
For this service of giving that you perform not only makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through many givings of thanks to God;
seeing that through the proof given by this service, they glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Good News of Christ, and for the liberality of your contribution to them and to all;
while they themselves also, with supplication on your behalf, yearn for you by reason of the exceeding grace of God in you.
Now thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!

footnotes.content: Paul says it's 'unnecessary' to write about giving to the saints—but he's writing anyway. Sometimes we think we don't need to ask or remind, but love speaks up anyway. His care for both the givers and the receivers shows in every word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul boasts about the Corinthians' 'readiness' to the Macedonians—he's proud of their willingness, and that pride becomes a spur to faithfulness. Sometimes when someone believes in us aloud, we become who they believed we were.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He's sent brothers ahead so his 'boasting' won't turn out empty. Pride in another's generosity only holds if the generosity is real. Paul is careful that words match deeds—character built on alignment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fear here is 'disappointment'—not shame exactly, but the hurt of promised readiness that crumbles when the moment comes. Paul wants to spare the Corinthians the regret of their own unfaithfulness, not out of shame but out of love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul asks the brothers to arrange the gift ahead of time 'as a matter of generosity, and not of greediness.' The heart's intention matters as much as the act itself—abundance of spirit, not mere obligation. A wise pastor knows the gift's worth lies in the giver's freedom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly'—not as punishment, but as the grain of how the world is made. We receive what we send out; the Lord simply lets the seed grow according to its kind. Generosity multiplies by its own nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'God loves a cheerful giver'—not the perfectionist, not the guilty obliged, but the one who gives because it brings joy. The Lord looks not at the size of the gift but at the lightness of the heart that sends it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'God is able to make all grace abound to you'—Paul moves from human giving to divine sufficiency. What frees us to give is the certainty that God has already given us enough, and will keep us enough. Grace abounding becomes the engine of our own generosity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul quotes Psalm 112:9: 'He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor. His righteousness remains forever.' The righteous heart scatters; its legacy is not wealth but blessing. When we give, we echo the character of God Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God 'supplies seed to the sower and bread for food'—He provides both the means to give and the nourishment to live. The Lord thinks of us in both directions: keeping us alive and equipping us to sow. His provision never runs dry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Being 'enriched in everything to all liberality' doesn't mean being wealthy—it means having enough to turn outward without counting. The riches that matter are the ones that flow; hoarded wealth is a slow death, but shared grace multiplies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Giving 'not only makes up for lack among the saints, but abounds also through many givings of thanks to God.' Generosity is a two-way door: it meets physical need and opens a floodgate of gratitude. Both giver and receiver are changed by thankfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The recipients 'glorify God for the obedience of your confession to the Good News.' When we give, we're confessing aloud that we believe in the Gospel—that Jesus changes how we hold what we own. Our wallet is a sermon.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poor saints pray for the Corinthians 'by reason of the exceeding grace of God in you.' Generosity doesn't just meet need; it creates bond. The recipients hold the givers in their prayers, and that spiritual knot holds tighter than any contract.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this close: 'Thanks be to God for his unspeakable gift!'—Christ, of course, is the gift no words can hold. Every act of giving in His name is a whisper of gratitude for a grace so big it broke time itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
